etymology: From Chinese gung ho (Mandarin gong he), "work together," a slogan of the Chinese Industrial Cooperatives of the late 1930s. Marine Lt. Col. Evans F. Carlson, who had observed Chinese forces in the 1930s, adopted it as the motto of his 2nd Marine Raider Battalion in 1942, and the 1943 film Gung Ho!, about the Raiders’ Makin Island raid, made it national. By the later 1940s it had come to mean eager, zealous, all in — and sometimes overzealous.
biblical_def: When Grandpa’s generation said a man was gung-ho, they meant he was all in — first up in the morning, first to volunteer, the last to quit. The word came from the Marines, and the Marines got it from China: it was a slogan meaning "work together," which Colonel Evans Carlson gave his Raiders in 1942. Notice that: the original gung-ho was not one man’s fire but a whole unit pulling as one. Scripture likes that. "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour" (Ecc 4:9), and "a threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecc 4:12). When Nehemiah’s people rebuilt Jerusalem’s wall under threat, it rose fast, "for the people had a mind to work" (Neh 4:6). Paul wanted the church to stand "with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel" (Php 1:27). There is a warning too. Zeal without wisdom can run a man into trouble, and Paul grieved over people who had "a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom 10:2). The perfect example of right zeal is Christ Himself, who cleansed His Father’s house so that His disciples remembered, "The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (Joh 2:17). He was all in for His Father’s glory, all the way to the cross, and He did it to make one people out of many. A Christian should be gung-ho in the first sense — eager, wholehearted, and pulling together.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII Marine Corps, from a Chinese slogan meaning "work together") for zealous, wholehearted, all in — zeal Scripture commends when it pulls together and is according to knowledge (Rom 10:2).
webster_full: GUNG-HO, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; Marine Corps, from Chinese "work together") Zealously enthusiastic; eager and wholehearted, sometimes to excess. "The new lieutenant is awful gung-ho."
Decode for families: gung-ho first meant "work together" — the best zeal is shared, and it knows what it is zealous for.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Joh 2:17
And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
corruption_summary: An honourable word for wholehearted effort; the only caution is zeal without knowledge — the eager man who outruns wisdom or his comrades.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with being gung-ho. The word was born in a Marine battalion that trained hard and fought together, and its first meaning — work together — is a fine one for any family or church. Scripture praises a people with a mind to work (Neh 4:6).

The word later picked up an edge: the gung-ho man can be the one who charges ahead without thinking, or who makes everyone else’s life hard by his eagerness. Paul’s warning fits him — zeal not according to knowledge (Rom 10:2). The cure is not less zeal but zeal aimed rightly, and shared.
roots_summary: Chinese gong he (work together; 1930s cooperative slogan) → 1942 motto of Carlson’s 2nd Marine Raiders → 1943 film Gung Ho! → 1940s American slang (zealous, all in).
roots_lines: Chinese gong (work) + he (together, in harmony)
Late 1930s: slogan of the Chinese Industrial Cooperatives
1942: motto of Lt. Col. Evans Carlson’s 2nd Marine Raider Battalion
1943: the film Gung Ho! spreads the word
Later 1940s–: gung-ho — eager, zealous, sometimes overzealous
usage: "Uncle Walt was so gung-ho about the church roof he had the shingles up before the deacons finished voting."
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour (Ecc 4:9).
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work (Neh 4:6).

etymology: From military radio procedure. In the US and British phonetic alphabets of the Second World War the letter R was spoken "Roger," and in radio procedure R stood for "received." So "Roger" meant "message received and understood." Pilots and radiomen carried it home, and it became everyday talk for "OK, got it." The pairing roger, wilco (will comply) belongs to the same procedure. Later phonetic alphabets replaced Roger with Romeo, but the word stayed.
biblical_def: When a bomber pilot over Europe heard his orders on the radio, he answered with one word: "Roger." It meant, I heard you, I understood you. Add "wilco" and it meant, I will comply. Your grandfather may still say it at the supper table when Grandma asks him to take out the trash. It is a good word, and Scripture has a great deal to say about the thing it names: hearing and answering. When God called the boy Samuel in the night, Samuel answered, "Speak; for thy servant heareth" (1Sa 3:10). When God asked who would go for Him, Isaiah answered, "Here am I; send me" (Isa 6:8). That is roger and wilco together. The Lord wants plain answers from His people: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37) — no hedging, no fine print. And He wants the second half too. A radioman who says roger and then ignores the order has not really received it. James says, "be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves" (Jas 1:22). Jesus said of those who belong to Him, "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me" (Joh 10:27). Hearing, knowing, following — that is the whole Christian life in three words. When the Lord speaks in His Word, the right answer is still the old one: roger, wilco.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII radio procedure; R for "received") for message received, understood, agreed — the plain answer Samuel gave the LORD (1Sa 3:10), which Scripture asks us to follow with obedience.
webster_full: ROGER, interj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; from WWII radio procedure) Message received and understood; OK, agreed. "Roger — I’ll be home by six." With wilco, "will comply."
Decode for families: roger means I heard you; wilco means I will do it — God wants both.
scriptures: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
Isa 6:8
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
corruption_summary: A wholesome word of plain acknowledgment; the only snare is the "roger" that hears and does not do.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in roger. It is clear, honest, and short — very nearly the "Yea, yea" that Jesus asked for (Mat 5:37). A family that answers each other with a cheerful roger is doing better than most.

The only caution is the empty roger: the child who says "got it" and does not move, the Christian who hears a sermon and forgets it by lunch. James calls that self-deception (Jas 1:22). A true roger is followed by wilco.
roots_summary: WWII phonetic alphabet Roger = R → radio procedure R = "received" → roger (message received, understood) → postwar everyday "OK, got it."
roots_lines: English name Roger — used for the letter R in WWII phonetic alphabets
Radio procedure: R — "received"
1940s: roger — message received and understood; wilco — will comply
Later alphabets: Romeo replaces Roger for R
Postwar–: roger — everyday "OK, got it"
usage: "Grandma told Grandpa to wipe his boots, and he said, ‘Roger, wilco,’ the way he did for fifty years."
Speak; for thy servant heareth (1Sa 3:10).
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (Joh 10:27).

etymology: From Chinese Pidgin English chow-chow (a mixture; food), heard in the China trade and recorded in American English by the mid-1800s, especially in California. The Army and Navy took it up, and by the World Wars chow was the standard service word for a meal: chow line, chow hall, chow time. Returning servicemen made it household slang.
biblical_def: Ask a veteran what he remembers about the service and sooner or later he will tell you about the chow — powdered eggs, Spam, K-rations, and once in a while a Thanksgiving dinner served off a tailgate that he still talks about. Chow means food, plain and simple, and the chow line is one of the great levelers: the private and the sergeant both stand in it. Scripture takes food more seriously than we might think. Jesus taught us to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Mat 6:11), because every meal is a gift from the Father. Paul wrote, "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1Co 10:31) — so even chow can be eaten to God’s glory, with thanks. The first Christians "did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46), sharing tables from house to house. And after His resurrection the risen Lord cooked breakfast on a beach for tired fishermen and called to them, "Come and dine" (Joh 21:12). The deepest thing the Bible says about food is that it points beyond itself. Jesus said, "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger" (Joh 6:35). Chow fills a man until supper. Christ fills him forever. So say grace over the chow, whatever it is, and thank the One who feeds both body and soul.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (from Chinese Pidgin, American by the 1850s; universal in WWII service) for food or a meal — daily bread Scripture teaches us to ask for and eat to the glory of God (1Co 10:31), pointing to the bread of life.
webster_full: CHOW, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; service word from 19th-century Pidgin chow-chow) Food; a meal. "Chow’s on!" Also chow line, chow hall, chow down.
Decode for families: chow is just food — and every bite is a gift worth saying grace over.
scriptures: Mat 6:11
Give us this day our daily bread.
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord.
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
corruption_summary: A wholesome, homely word for food; the only cautions are the old ones about food itself — ingratitude and gluttony.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in chow needs correcting. It is the plain word of men who were grateful for a hot meal, and Grandpa calling the family to supper with "Chow time!" is a happy thing.

The word does invite the oldest lessons about eating. A meal received without thanks forgets the Giver (Mat 6:11), and a meal eaten without restraint becomes gluttony. Eaten with gladness and thanksgiving, as the first Christians ate (Act 2:46), chow is a small sacrament of God’s kindness.
roots_summary: Chinese Pidgin chow-chow (mixture; food) → mid-1800s American chow (food) → Army and Navy word → WWII universal service slang → household word.
roots_lines: Chinese Pidgin English chow-chow — a mixture; food
Mid-1800s American (California): chow — food
Army and Navy: chow — a meal; chow line, chow hall
1940s: universal service slang; carried home by veterans
usage: "Grandpa still hollers ‘Chow time!’ up the stairs, and we still come running."
Give us this day our daily bread (Mat 6:11).
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God (1Co 10:31).

etymology: US Army slang for an infantry soldier, recorded by the early 1940s and of uncertain origin. Soldiers used it of themselves, with a mixture of grumbling and pride, for the foot soldier who walked, dug, and endured; it was common in wartime newspapers and cartoons and in the memoirs of the men who served.
biblical_def: In 1944 a dogface was a foot soldier — the GI who walked where the trucks could not go, dug his own hole, slept in the mud, and ate cold rations. The men called themselves dogfaces with a grumble and a grin. It was not a proud title, and that was the point: the infantryman knew he did the hardest, plainest work of the war and got the least credit for it. Scripture honours that kind of man. Paul used him as a picture of the Christian life: "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3). When soldiers came to John the Baptist and asked what they should do, he did not tell them to quit; he said, "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages" (Luk 3:14). A Roman centurion understood faith better than anyone in Israel because he understood orders: "I am a man under authority" (Mat 8:9). The dogface was looked down on, and there is One who knows that better than any soldier. Christ was "despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief" (Isa 53:3). He took the lowest place on purpose, and He said, "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (Joh 15:13). Then He did it. Many a dogface did the same for the man in the next hole. When your grandfather or great-grandfather says he was just a dogface, thank him — and thank the Lord who honours the lowly.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII Army) for the infantryman, the plain foot soldier — a lowly name for hard, faithful service, which Scripture honours in the good soldier who endures hardness (2Ti 2:3).
webster_full: DOGFACE, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; US Army) An infantry soldier; a foot soldier, used by the men of themselves. "We were just dogfaces — we walked the whole way."
Decode for families: a dogface was a foot soldier — the man who did the hardest work and asked for the least credit.
scriptures: Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
Luk 3:14
And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
Mat 8:9
For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it.
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
corruption_summary: A self-deprecating soldiers’ word, not a sinful one; the only care is to use it with the respect the men who earned it deserve.
corruption_paragraphs: The infantrymen who called themselves dogfaces were not running themselves down so much as telling the truth about hard service with a soldier’s humor. There is nothing in the word to condemn, and much in the men to honour.

The care belongs to those who were not there. A word a soldier uses of himself is not a word for others to use in contempt. Grandchildren who hear it should hear it as Scripture would have them hear it: as the name of a man who endured hardness (2Ti 2:3) and, often enough, laid his life on the line for his friends (Joh 15:13).
roots_summary: English dog + face → early 1940s US Army slang (the infantryman, used of themselves) → WWII newspapers, cartoons, and memoirs → a veterans’ word.
roots_lines: English dog — long used in slang for a lowly, hard-used fellow
Early 1940s US Army: dogface — an infantry soldier; origin uncertain
1940s: soldiers’ self-name, common in wartime papers and cartoons
Postwar: a veterans’ word for the foot soldier
usage: "Great-Grandpa said he was just a dogface who walked from Normandy to the Rhine. He said ‘just’ like it was nothing."
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ (2Ti 2:3).
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13).

etymology: From German Flak, an abbreviation of Fliegerabwehrkanone, "aircraft-defense cannon." Allied airmen of the Second World War used it for the bursting anti-aircraft fire that filled the sky over enemy targets; flak jackets and flak suits were armour against it. The figurative sense, criticism or hostile reaction ("he took a lot of flak"), was in American use by the 1960s.
biblical_def: When a bomber crew flew over Germany, the worst of the trip was often the flak — black bursts of anti-aircraft fire that rocked the plane and tore through its skin. A crew could not shoot back at flak; they could only hold their course and fly through it. Many did not come home, and the men who did seldom talked about it. After the war the word came down to earth, and now we say a man takes flak when he is criticized. Both senses meet in Scripture. The Christian will take flak. Jesus said so: "Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake" (Mat 5:11). God gives armour for it: "taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked" (Eph 6:16). And He gives a steady heart: "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day" (Psa 91:5). But not all flak comes from the enemy. Some criticism is deserved, and Scripture is blunt about the man who will not hear it: "he that hateth reproof is brutish" (Pro 12:1). The wise man listens first and answers gently, for "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Pro 15:1). Christ took more flak than any man who ever lived, and He held His course: "when he was reviled, reviled not again" (1Pe 2:23). He went straight through it to the cross, for us.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII airmen, from German Flak) for anti-aircraft fire, and later for criticism — flak Scripture tells us to meet with the shield of faith (Eph 6:16), a teachable ear, and a soft answer.
webster_full: FLAK, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWII airmen, from German) 1. Anti-aircraft fire. "The flak was so thick you could walk on it." 2. (from the 1960s) Criticism, hostile reaction. "He took a lot of flak for that."
Decode for families: flak was the fire bombers flew through; now it means criticism — hold your course, and listen if it is true.
scriptures: Mat 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Eph 6:16
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.
Psa 91:5
Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day;
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_summary: A soldiers’ word honestly come by; the only care is in its later sense — neither to return flak for flak, nor to wave off criticism that is deserved.
corruption_paragraphs: The first sense of flak is a hard memory for the men who flew through it, and children should hear it with respect. There is nothing sinful in the word itself.

The figurative sense carries two temptations. One is to answer criticism with more of the same; Christ, reviled, reviled not again (1Pe 2:23). The other is to treat all criticism as enemy fire, when some of it is a friend’s reproof that only a brutish man refuses (Pro 12:1). A Christian sorts the two, and answers both softly (Pro 15:1).
roots_summary: German Fliegerabwehrkanone (aircraft-defense cannon) → Flak → WWII Allied airmen’s word (anti-aircraft fire) → 1960s American (criticism).
roots_lines: German Flieger (flyer) + Abwehr (defense) + Kanone (cannon)
Flak — German abbreviation for anti-aircraft guns
WWII Allied airmen: flak — anti-aircraft fire; flak jacket
By the 1960s: flak — criticism, hostile reaction
usage: "Grandpa took a lot of flak at the church meeting for wanting to fix the roof first. He smiled and said he had seen worse flak."
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger (Pro 15:1).
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked (Eph 6:16).

etymology: American GI graffiti of the Second World War: the words "Kilroy was here," usually with a cartoon of a bald, long-nosed face peering over a wall, appeared wherever American servicemen went — on ships, barracks walls, bridges, and beaches. The drawing is shared with the British wartime cartoon "Mr. Chad." The origin is disputed: several men have been put forward as the original Kilroy, and none is proven.
biblical_def: Wherever American servicemen went in the Second World War, Kilroy had already been there. The little bald fellow peeking over a wall, with the words "Kilroy was here," turned up on ships’ bulkheads, barracks walls, bridges, and beaches all over the world. Nobody knows for sure who Kilroy was; the joke was that he always got there first. Men far from home, often frightened, scrawled it to say, We came this way — remember us. That is a very human wish. Men have always wanted to leave their mark: at Babel they said, "let us make us a name" (Gen 11:4), and the psalm says of the proud that "they call their lands after their own names" (Psa 49:11). Most marks fade. But there is One who was truly everywhere first. David asked, "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" (Psa 139:7). Jacob woke in a lonely place and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not" (Gen 28:16). And God did more than leave a sign; He came Himself: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (Joh 1:14) — God was here, in Bethlehem, in Galilee, on the cross. Now Christ promises every believer, wherever duty sends him, "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world" (Mat 28:20). A GI in a foxhole was never really alone. The Lord was there before Kilroy.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII GI graffiti) for the tag and cartoon that announced American servicemen had passed by — a wish to be remembered, answered by the God who is everywhere first and promises, lo, I am with you alway (Mat 28:20).
webster_full: KILROY WAS HERE, phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWII GI graffiti) A tag, usually with a cartoon face peeking over a wall, left wherever American servicemen passed. "We got to the bridge and, sure enough, Kilroy was here."
Decode for families: Kilroy was the GIs’ joke that someone always got there first — the Lord really does.
scriptures: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
Gen 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.
corruption_summary: A harmless wartime joke; the only thing to examine is graffiti itself — marking what belongs to others — and the deeper wish to make a name for oneself.
corruption_paragraphs: Kilroy was mostly a morale joke, and much of it was chalked on walls in places the war had already wrecked. Grandchildren should not take it as license to write on what is not theirs; defacing a neighbour’s property is no joke at home.

The deeper lesson is the wish behind it. Babel wanted a name (Gen 11:4), and every generation wants to be remembered. The Christian’s comfort is not that his name is scrawled somewhere but that he is known by the God who was already there (Psa 139:7) and who came Himself in Christ (Joh 1:14).
roots_summary: Surname Kilroy (origin of the joke disputed) + the peeking-face cartoon (shared with British "Mr. Chad") → WWII GI graffiti → postwar byword for "someone got here first."
roots_lines: Irish surname Kilroy — the original Kilroy unknown and disputed
Early 1940s: "Kilroy was here" chalked by American servicemen worldwide
The peeking-face doodle — shared with the British "Mr. Chad"
Postwar: a byword for having been somewhere first
usage: "Grandpa took us to the war memorial and showed us a little Kilroy carved on the base. He laughed, and then he got quiet."
Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not (Gen 28:16).
Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence (Psa 139:7).

etymology: Royal Air Force slang of uncertain origin, recorded around 1940–41: a gremlin was an imaginary imp blamed for unexplained mechanical failures in aircraft. American airmen picked it up, and Roald Dahl, himself a former RAF pilot, popularized it in his 1943 children’s book The Gremlins. Since the war any mysterious glitch has been a gremlin.
biblical_def: When an engine quit for no reason, a gauge went haywire, or a bolt worked loose that every mechanic swore was tight, the RAF crews of 1941 blamed the gremlins — tiny imps who rode along on bombers and made mischief. American airmen picked them up too. It was a joke, mostly, and a useful one: it let tired, frightened men laugh at things they could not control. But the joke points at two deep habits of the human heart. The first is blaming someone else. It is as old as Eden: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Gen 3:12). Adam blamed Eve and, in the same breath, blamed God. Scripture will not let us do that: "every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed" (Jas 1:14), and "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the LORD" (Pro 19:3). The second habit is imagining that the world is run by luck and mischief. The Bible says no little imp runs anything. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33). Not even a sparrow falls "without your Father" (Mat 10:29). So a Christian can fix the engine, own his mistakes, and rest in the Father’s care. There are no gremlins — but there is a Savior who took on Himself the blame we try to pass to others.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (RAF and American airmen, early 1940s) for the imaginary imp blamed for mechanical failures — a joke that exposes the old habits of shifting blame (Gen 3:12) and crediting luck instead of the Father’s providence (Pro 16:33).
webster_full: GREMLIN, n. (Silent Generation slang, early 1940s; RAF, then American airmen) An imaginary imp blamed for mechanical failures; any unexplained glitch. "Gremlins got into the radio again."
Decode for families: gremlins are make-believe troublemakers — the real lessons are to own our mistakes and trust God’s care.
scriptures: Gen 3:12
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.
Jas 1:14
But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
Pro 19:3
The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the LORD.
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
corruption_summary: A joke more than a belief; what it carries is blame-shifting and a playful superstition that hands the world to luck rather than to God’s providence.
corruption_paragraphs: The airmen who talked about gremlins did not, for the most part, believe in them. It was gallows humor in a dangerous trade, and nobody should be scolded for it. Still, jokes teach, and this one teaches two bad habits if it is taken seriously.

The first is passing blame, which began in Eden (Gen 3:12) and which Scripture refuses (Jas 1:14). The second is the half-serious notion that unseen mischief runs things. The Bible gives the world a Father instead: the lot falls as He disposes (Pro 16:33), and no sparrow falls without Him (Mat 10:29).
roots_summary: RAF slang of uncertain origin (c. 1940–41) → American airmen’s word → 1943 The Gremlins (Roald Dahl) → any mysterious glitch.
roots_lines: Origin uncertain — RAF slang recorded around 1940–41
WWII airmen: gremlin — an imp blamed for mechanical trouble
1943: Roald Dahl’s The Gremlins popularizes the word
Postwar–: gremlin — any unexplained malfunction
usage: "Grandpa says the gremlins got into the lawn mower again. Grandma says the gremlin forgot to change the oil."
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).
But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed (Jas 1:14).

etymology: American military aviators’ slang for being killed, especially in a crash. The shorter buy it, to be killed, goes back to the First World War; the full phrase buy the farm is recorded in print from the 1950s. The origin of the farm is uncertain; a common explanation — that a serviceman’s life insurance would pay off his family’s farm — is unproven.
biblical_def: Airmen had a quiet way of talking about death. A pilot who went down did not die; he bought it, or later, he bought the farm. Nobody is sure where the farm came from. What is sure is why the men talked that way: death was close every day, and a plain word for it was too heavy to carry around. Grandchildren should hear that with respect. Many of those men did not come home, and they gave their lives for us. Scripture does not use euphemisms about death: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Heb 9:27). Moses prayed, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). But the Bible also says something no airman’s slang could say: for the believer, death is not the end of the road but the way home. "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints" (Psa 116:15). Paul wrote, "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Php 1:21). And here the old phrase turns out to have a gospel in it. Jesus told of a man who found treasure hid in a field and "for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field" (Mat 13:44). Christ is the One who truly bought the field: He gave everything, His own life, to purchase His people. Because He died and rose, those who trust Him can face their last day without a euphemism and without fear.
webster_summary: Military aviators’ slang (from WWI buy it; in print by the 1950s) for being killed — a soldier’s gentle euphemism for a hard thing, answered in Scripture by the plain truth of death (Heb 9:27) and the hope of Christ.
webster_full: BUY THE FARM, v. phr. (Silent Generation slang; military aviators, from WWI buy it, in print by the 1950s) To be killed, especially in a crash; to die. "He bought the farm over the Channel."

Webster (1828) — FARM, noun 2. In the United States, a portion or tract of land, consisting usually of grass land, meadow, pasture, tillage and woodland, cultivated by one man and usually owned by him in fee. A like tract of land under lease is called a farm; but most cultivators are proprietors of the land, and called farmers. A tract of new land, covered with forest, if intended to be cultivated by one man as owner, is also called a farm A man goes into the new States, or into the unsettled country, to buy a farm that is, land for a farm
Decode for families: bought the farm means died — say it gently, and remember the men it was said of.
scriptures: Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
corruption_summary: An honourable soldiers’ euphemism, not a sin; the care is to speak it with respect and not to let a soft word hide the hard truth of death, which only Christ answers.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wicked in buy the farm. Men who faced death daily needed a way to speak of it, and a light phrase let them do their duty. It should never be used flippantly by those who did not stand where they stood.

The Christian lesson is about euphemism itself. Soft words can help us bear grief, but they can also help us avoid thinking about death at all. Scripture asks us to number our days (Psa 90:12) and to look death in the face — not with dread, but with Christ, for whom to die is gain (Php 1:21).
roots_summary: WWI buy it (to be killed) → military aviators’ buy the farm (in print by the 1950s; origin of "farm" uncertain) → general American euphemism for dying.
roots_lines: English buy + farm (Latin firma, a fixed payment; later a leased or owned tract)
WWI: buy it — to be killed
Military aviation: buy the farm — to die in a crash; recorded in print from the 1950s
Later: bought the farm — general American euphemism for death
usage: "Grandpa doesn’t say his friend bought the farm the way people do in movies. He says it slow, and he says the man’s whole name."
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psa 116:15).
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Php 1:21).

etymology: British Army slang of the First World War, recorded from 1915, from Hindi and Urdu khush (pleasant, happy), picked up by soldiers who had served in India. A cushy job was a soft, safe posting. The word crossed into American use and was common in the service by the 1940s; it has stayed in everyday speech for any easy, comfortable situation.
biblical_def: In the service, everyone wanted a cushy job — a desk in a rear area, a posting far from the shooting, a sergeant who did not care much. After the war the word came home: a cushy job pays well and asks little. Wanting a little ease is not wicked; the Lord gives His people rest. Jesus Himself said, "my yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Mat 11:30). But Scripture warns about loving ease more than duty. The prophet thundered, "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion" (Amo 6:1) — people comfortable while the nation fell apart. Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Luk 12:19). That night God called him a fool, and his soul was required of him. Paul told young Timothy to expect the opposite of cushy: "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3). And Paul himself, who had known prisons and shipwrecks, wrote, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11). The Christian does not hunt for the cushy post. He takes the post God gives, easy or hard, and is content in it. And he knows that the easy yoke Christ offers was bought at the hardest price: the Lord took no cushy road, but the road to the cross.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (British Army WWI, from Hindi khush; common in 1940s American service) for an easy, comfortable job or posting — ease Scripture permits but warns against loving (Amo 6:1), calling us to contentment in any state.
webster_full: CUSHY, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; British Army from 1915, from Hindi khush) Easy, comfortable, undemanding, of a job or posting. "He landed a cushy job in the quartermaster’s office."
Decode for families: cushy means easy — fine to enjoy, dangerous to love more than duty.
scriptures: For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Amo 6:1
Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!
And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
corruption_summary: A neutral word for comfort; the snare is the love of ease that dodges duty and settles down while others bear the load.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no sin in a comfortable job, and Scripture never calls ease evil in itself; rest is God’s gift. A grandfather who finally landed a cushy job after hard years earned it honestly.

The danger is in the seeking. The man whose chief aim is the cushy post will dodge hard duty, leave the heavy work to others, and grow at ease in Zion (Amo 6:1). Scripture puts contentment in its place (Php 4:11): take what God gives, work it faithfully, and do not make comfort your god.
roots_summary: Hindi/Urdu khush (pleasant) → 1915 British Army cushy (soft, safe) → 1940s American service slang → everyday "easy, comfortable."
roots_lines: Persian, Hindi, Urdu khush — pleasant, happy
1915: British Army cushy — a soft, safe job or posting
1940s: common in American service slang
Postwar–: cushy — any easy, comfortable situation
usage: "Grandpa said his cousin had a cushy job stateside the whole war, and he never once held it against him — but he never let him forget it either."
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Mat 11:30).
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ (2Ti 2:3).

etymology: A gold brick was first a swindle: a brick of base metal gilded to pass for solid gold, sold to the gullible in nineteenth-century America. The Army turned the word on its own shirkers — the soldier who looked as if he were working but was not — and goldbrick as a noun and verb (to loaf, to dodge duty) is recorded from the First World War era and was universal in the Second.
biblical_def: Every outfit in the war had a goldbrick — the fellow who always had a sore foot when there was digging to do, who found a broom to hold whenever the sergeant walked by and somehow never swept anything. The name came from an old swindle: a brick painted gold to look like treasure. A goldbrick looked like a soldier, but inside he was lead. Scripture has a word for him, and it is not a compliment: "He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster" (Pro 18:9). Solomon sends the shirker to school with an insect: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Pro 6:6). Paul tells the church plainly, "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10). And he names the goldbrick’s exact sin: working "with eyeservice, as menpleasers" (Col 3:22) — only when the boss is watching. The cure is to remember who the real Boss is: "Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ" (Col 3:24). God is always watching, not to catch us but because He cares about our work. And Christ is the perfect opposite of the goldbrick. He finished every task the Father gave Him, down to the last, and said on the cross, It is finished. The Christian works hard not to earn grace but because he has received it.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (Army, WWI era; universal in WWII) for a shirker, or to loaf on the job — from the gilded-lead swindle brick, and the very eyeservice Scripture condemns (Col 3:22) in those who serve the Lord Christ.
webster_full: GOLDBRICK, n. and v. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; Army from the WWI era) n. A shirker who looks busy but is not. v. To loaf, to dodge duty. "Quit goldbricking and grab a shovel."
Decode for families: a goldbrick looks like gold and is really lead — work the same whether anyone is watching or not.
scriptures: Pro 18:9
He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.
Pro 6:6
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Col 3:22
Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:
Col 3:24
Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.
corruption_summary: The word names a real sin plainly: sloth dressed up as work, eyeservice that labors only when watched, and the burden it lays on others.
corruption_paragraphs: Unlike many slang words, goldbrick does not need its sin uncovered; it names one. The goldbrick’s fault is not only laziness but deceit — he looks busy, and his comrades carry his share. Scripture calls the slothful worker brother to the waster (Pro 18:9).

The word is useful in a family. Children learn early how to look busy when Mother walks by. The answer is not a sharper sergeant but a deeper reason: we serve the Lord Christ (Col 3:24), who sees the broom that never sweeps and the work done faithfully in secret.
roots_summary: 19th-century American gold brick (gilded swindle brick) → WWI-era Army goldbrick (a shirker; to loaf) → universal in WWII → civilian slang for dodging work.
roots_lines: 19th-century America: gold brick — a gilded fake sold as solid gold
WWI-era Army: goldbrick — a shirker who only looks like he works
1940s: goldbrick, goldbricking — universal service slang
Postwar–: any loafer on the job
usage: "Grandpa caught me leaning on the rake and said, ‘No goldbricking in this outfit.’ Then he picked up a rake too."
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise (Pro 6:6).
Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ (Col 3:24).

etymology: US Navy and Marine Corps slang of uncertain origin. Skivvy for a sailor’s undershirt is recorded before the war, and the plural skivvies for underwear — skivvy shirt and skivvy shorts — was common by the Second World War; returning servicemen made it household slang. The British skivvy, a household drudge, is a separate word.
biblical_def: In the Navy, a sailor’s underwear was his skivvies — skivvy shirt and skivvy shorts, folded just so in his locker for inspection. The word came home with the sailors, and Grandpa may still call his underwear skivvies. It is a homely, harmless word, and it gives a family a good place to talk about something the Bible treats with care: clothing and modesty. The first clothes in history were a kind of underwear. When Adam and Eve sinned, "they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons" (Gen 3:7). Shame came with sin, and they tried to cover it themselves. The fig leaves were not enough, and God, in mercy, did better: "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them" (Gen 3:21). An animal died so that they could be covered. That is the first picture of the gospel. Clothing, even the plainest, is a daily reminder that we need covering and that God provides it. So the Christian keeps his skivvies where they belong — under his clothes, not on parade. Jesus tells us not to worry about what we shall wear, for "your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things" (Mat 6:32). And He offers the covering that matters most: "white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear" (Rev 3:18). Christ’s righteousness is the one garment no sinner can sew for himself.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (US Navy and Marine Corps, common by WWII) for underwear — a homely word that opens the Bible’s teaching on modesty and on God covering our shame, from the coats of skins (Gen 3:21) to the white raiment of Christ.
webster_full: SKIVVIES, n. pl. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; US Navy and Marine Corps) Underwear; a skivvy shirt (undershirt) and skivvy shorts. "Fold your skivvies for inspection."
Decode for families: skivvies are underwear — and every piece of clothing reminds us that God covers our shame.
scriptures: Gen 3:7
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
Mat 6:32
(For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.
Rev 3:18

I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
corruption_summary: A plain, harmless word for underwear; the only care is the modesty that keeps what is private private.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with skivvies. It is a sailor’s practical word, and a barracks full of men in skivvies at reveille was nothing anyone thought twice about.

The care is modesty. What is meant to be under the clothes belongs under the clothes in mixed company, in photographs, and in public. Scripture ties clothing to the shame sin brought and to God’s merciful covering (Gen 3:21), so even our underwear can remind us of the gospel.
roots_summary: Navy skivvy (undershirt; origin uncertain) → skivvies (underwear, common by WWII) → household slang via returning servicemen.
roots_lines: Origin uncertain — US Navy skivvy, an undershirt, recorded before the war
1940s: skivvies, skivvy shirt, skivvy shorts — Navy and Marine Corps
Postwar: household slang for underwear
Distinct from British skivvy — a household drudge
usage: "Grandpa still folds his skivvies in perfect squares. He says the Navy never let him stop."
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them (Gen 3:21).
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked (Gen 3:7).

etymology: Naval, from scuttled butt: a butt is a cask, and a scuttled one has a hole cut in it. The ship’s drinking-water cask, with its opening for the dipper, was the scuttlebutt (recorded from the early 1800s), and sailors gathered there to drink and trade rumors, as office workers later did at the water cooler. The sense of rumor or gossip is recorded from the early 1900s and was universal in the Navy and Marine Corps by the Second World War.
biblical_def: On a ship, the scuttlebutt was the water cask, and around it the sailors heard everything first: where the ship was going, who was getting promoted, which officer was in trouble. So scuttlebutt came to mean rumor. In the war, scuttlebutt ran wild — the ship was going home, the ship was going to Japan, the war would be over by Christmas. Most of it was wrong. Scripture is sober about rumor. God’s law says, "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" (Lev 19:16), and "Thou shalt not raise a false report" (Exo 23:1). Solomon knew why rumor spreads: "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly" (Pro 18:8) — we like the taste of them. He also knew how to stop it: "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20). A Christian does not have to pass on every piece of scuttlebutt; he can let it die at his feet. And the water cask has a better lesson still. Jesus met a woman at a village well, the place where everyone came to draw water and hear the news, and offered her better water than gossip: "the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life" (Joh 4:14). Christ’s words are not rumor but truth, and they never run dry.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (Navy and Marines, from the ship’s water cask; rumor sense from the early 1900s) for rumor and gossip — talebearing Scripture forbids (Lev 19:16), answered by the living water of Christ’s true word (Joh 4:14).
webster_full: SCUTTLEBUTT, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; Navy and Marine Corps) 1. The ship’s drinking-water cask or fountain. 2. Rumor, gossip. "The scuttlebutt says we’re headed home."

Webster (1828) — SCUTTLE, verb transitive [from the noun.] 1. To cut large holes through the bottom or sides of a ship for any purpose. 2. To sink by making holes through the bottom; as, to scuttle a ship.
Decode for families: scuttlebutt is rumor — let it stop with you unless you know it is true and kind.
scriptures: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
Exo 23:1
Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
Pro 18:8
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
corruption_summary: The word names a real fault plainly: rumor and talebearing, which wound reputations and stir strife whether or not they turn out true.
corruption_paragraphs: Much scuttlebutt was harmless guessing about where the ship was bound, and sailors could hardly help wondering. But the word also covered the other kind of talk: who was in trouble, who had done what. Scripture forbids the talebearer (Lev 19:16) and the false report (Exo 23:1), and it knows why such words are tempting (Pro 18:8).

The cure is simple and hard: be the place where the rumor stops (Pro 26:20). A Christian can listen at the water cooler without adding wood to the fire, and can go to the better well for words that are true (Joh 4:14).
roots_summary: Scuttle (to cut a hole) + butt (cask) → scuttled butt (ship’s water cask, early 1800s) → early 1900s Navy (rumor) → WWII universal → everyday gossip.
roots_lines: Scuttle — to cut holes in a ship; a small hatchway
Butt — a large cask for liquids
Early 1800s: scuttlebutt — the ship’s water cask with a hole for the dipper
Early 1900s Navy: scuttlebutt — rumor traded at the cask
1940s–: universal Navy and Marine word; later, any gossip
usage: "Grandpa says the scuttlebutt on his ship had them going home every week for two years."
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth (Pro 26:20).
Thou shalt not raise a false report (Exo 23:1).
